title: Costs and benefits of bariatric surgery - Use of health and social services by patients with severe obesity
summary:
According to many studies, weight loss surgery is considered an effective and economically viable treatment for severe obesity. The findings to date are largely based on existing administrative data or theoretical calculations. Such approaches can, by their very nature, only provide a limited picture of how individuals actually use the services offered by the health and social welfare system. In particular, services outside the realm of medical treatment, such as welfare benefits or assistance in everyday life, are often not recorded.

This study addresses this issue and collects new data directly from those affected. To this end, people are asked about their use of health and social services in structured surveys. This allows a direct comparison of the costs incurred by individuals before and after planned surgery. On this basis, cost differences are to be accurately recorded and used to calculate whether and to what extent the operation is “worth it” from a societal perspective.

In addition, differences in perceived health-related quality of life and eating habits between individuals before and after surgery are examined in order to better assess the long-term benefits of the treatment.

Two groups are being studied: individuals who underwent such surgery between September 2015 and June 2018, and individuals who are severely overweight and are still in the preparation and assessment process prior to planned surgery. Both groups are interviewed in person using standardized interview guides about their use of social and medical services, their health-related quality of life, and their eating habits.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
preoperative body mass index (BMI) above 35 kg/m², indicating an obesity grade of 2 or 3
Exclusion criteria:
- insufficient German language skills
- intellectual disability
- developmental or learning disorders
- history of prior bariatric surgery
- current substance abuse
